passage:
Sunday. At lunch Harsha's father said, "Your cousin got into the science stream with a scholarship. Take a lesson." Harsha kept chewing. "Okay." Inside, he told himself he didn't care.

Thursday. His maths homework sat unopened for three days. When his friend asked, he shrugged. "Why bother?" He noticed the flatness: no anger, no shame, just a grey nothing where those used to be.

The following Saturday. In the kitchen, he asked himself: Do I not care, or have I just stopped feeling it? He suspected the second. He told his mother Gargi, quietly, "I stopped listening when Papa compares me. I think it still hurts." She put the ladle down and said, "Then tell me what it feels like."

qa.q: What did Harsha's father say his cousin got into?
qa.a: He said his cousin got into the science stream with a scholarship.

qa.q: What did Harsha suspect about his flat feeling by the following Saturday?
qa.a: He suspected he hadn't stopped caring but had stopped feeling, because the hurt was still there under the grey nothing.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next to avoid shutting down his effort altogether?
qa.a: He can keep the honest talk with Gargi going and go back to his homework, since numbness protects him only in the short term.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when Harsha said it still hurts?
qa.a: Probably surprised and ready to listen: she put the ladle down and asked him to tell her what it feels like.

grounding: Shows a teen who goes numb to comparisons and tells himself he does not care, then notices it and has one honest talk.

passage:
The bus had been stuck in the flooded underpass for forty minutes, and the board exam form was due at the school office before five. Afreen stared at the rain.
"Your Ammi called my Ammi again," Madhuri said carefully. "About Sameera's ranks."
Afreen shrugged. "Let her. I don't care anymore." She hadn't opened her chemistry book in two weeks. Every time Ammi mentioned Sameera, Afreen simply switched off, like a fan.
Madhuri waited. "Don't care, or don't want to feel it?"
Afreen opened her mouth to snap back, then didn't. Her throat was tight. "It still hurts," she said at last, very quietly. "I just stopped showing it. And stopped studying."
The bus lurched forward. Afreen checked the time: they would make it, barely.
"Tonight," she said, "I'm going to tell Ammi what the Sameera talk does to me. Just once, properly."

qa.q: How long had the bus been stuck in the underpass?
What was Afreen really feeling beneath her shrug?
qa.a: She was still hurt by Ammi's comparisons; she had gone numb to protect herself, and her tight throat showed the pain was still there.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen for her talk with Ammi?
qa.a: Tell Ammi calmly and specifically how the Sameera comparisons make her feel and that they pushed her to stop studying, then pick her chemistry book back up.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Afreen's 'I don't care'?
qa.a: Madhuri seems worried that Afreen is hiding pain behind indifference, which is why Madhuri asks gently instead of accepting the shrug.

grounding: A teen who has gone numb to a parent's comparisons checks whether she stopped caring or stopped feeling, and plans one honest talk.

passage:
Rashmi came home from her college hostel on Friday and noticed the change within an hour. At dinner in their Pune flat, Papa told the whole internship story again, then turned to Abhinav. "See what didi managed? You could too, if you tried."
Abhinav only said, "Hmm," and kept eating. No argument, no slammed door. Later Rashmi found his tuition notes still sealed in their plastic cover.
"You've stopped going," she said.
"What's the point? He compares anyway. I don't care now."
"Do you actually not care, or is it just easier not to feel it?"
Abhinav picked at the plastic for a long time. "It's easier," he admitted. "It still stings."
That night he knocked on Papa's door. "When you compare me with didi, I don't try harder. I stop trying," he said, voice shaking. Papa put down his newspaper and, for once, did not answer quickly.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi find Abhinav's tuition notes?
qa.a: Still sealed in their plastic cover.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he said he didn't care?
qa.a: He was hurt; he had gone numb because not feeling was easier than the sting of being compared with his sister.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what helped fix it?
qa.a: Abhinav had quietly given up on tuition; talking honestly with Papa once, instead of staying numb, started to fix it.

qa.q: How might Papa see the moment when Abhinav knocks on his door?
qa.a: Papa seems caught off guard and thoughtful; he had not realised his comparisons were making his son stop trying, so he pauses instead of answering quickly.

grounding: A teen who has gone numb to comparisons with his sister admits the hurt is still there and has one honest talk with his father.
